performers: Kerstin Thorborg, contralto; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Carl Martin Öhmann sings the tenor songs of the same concert)
intro: Girls pick lotus flowers by a river; horsemen ride past, leaving one girl watching after them. In this 1939 Amsterdam performance, Kerstin Thorborg sings both the gentle river scene and the breathless gallop that tears through it.

sections.label: A · Lotus flowers beside the river
sections.mNote: Flutes and muted violins open in G major

sections.label: B · The breeze lifts silk sleeves
sections.mNote: E major, unmuted violins and a solo violin

sections.label: C · Horsemen approach in the orchestra
sections.mNote: Brass, drums and mandolin turn the music into a march

sections.label: D · The singer catches the gallop
sections.mNote: The voice returns above quick strings and wooden timpani sticks

sections.mNote: Muted violins bring back the opening pace

sections.label: Coda · The girl looks after him
sections.mNote: Clarinet phrases and quiet violins outlast the voice

cues.title: Flowers by the river
cues.text: Trilling flutes and muted violins open a small, bright scene in G major. Thorborg’s first words place the girls at the water’s edge: “Junge Mädchen pflücken Blumen” — young girls pick flowers. The tune moves easily between bars of two and three beats.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 61–62: Comodo. Dolcissimo, the opening scoring and changing metre. Hans Bethge’s text as adapted by Mahler; our translation. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A lotus song, filtered twice
cues.text: The poem descends from Li Bai’s “Lotus-plucking Song”, set at Ruoye Brook near Shaoxing. The Marquis d’Hervey de Saint-Denys put it into French, Bethge into German verse, and Mahler retouched that. Li Bai’s original is far shorter than the song it became.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Von der Schönheit page, prints Li Bai’s poem and the location of Ruoye Brook, d’Hervey de Saint-Denys’s “Sur les bords du Jo-yeh”, Bethge’s text and Mahler’s alterations: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Schonheit.htm

cues.title: Sunlight and silk sleeves
cues.text: G major slips down to E major. The violins remove their mutes, and a solo violin floats above the words about the breeze lifting the girls’ sleeves. The harp’s quiet chords leave room for the long vocal line.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 63–64: rehearsal 5, a tempo (ruhiger), Dämpfer ab and the solo violin beside the Zephyr stanza.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horses before their riders
cues.text: Thorborg finishes on “Luft” — air — and the orchestra takes over. Stopped horns and muted trumpet and trombones begin to stir, with harp glissandi underneath. The horsemen arrive in the music well before the poem names them.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 65–70, rehearsal figures 7–10. Allmählich belebend follows the end of the breeze stanza; the voice remains silent until the horsemen stanza.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A mandolin among the drums
cues.text: The march adds a mandolin to its drums and brass. Tambourine rattles, bass drum and cymbal mark the stride, and both harps strike chords. The small plucked instrument is part of this boisterous parade.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 67–68: Più mosso subito (Marschmäßig), mandolin, two harps and percussion.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Thorborg names the riders
cues.text: The orchestra suddenly drops to piano for the singer’s return. “O sieh, was tummeln sich für schöne Knaben” — see the handsome boys romping there. Timpani played with wooden sticks keep the hooves moving as the vocal part grows faster and more crowded.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 70–77: Noch etwas flotter, p subito, Holzschlägel and the increasingly rapid horsemen stanza. Bethge’s text as adapted by Mahler; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler adds a cry
cues.text: In the horse’s lines Mahler adds a cry of his own: “Hei! Wie flattern im Taumel seine Mähnen, dampfen heiß die Nüstern!” — how his mane flies in a frenzy, how hot the nostrils steam. He also changes the girl’s pride from a lie, “Lüge”, to a pretence, “Verstellung”.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Von der Schönheit page, prints Bethge’s text beside Mahler’s alteration: the mane and nostril lines are absent from Bethge, and Lüge becomes Verstellung: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Schonheit.htm . Translation by the site.

cues.title: The river reappears
cues.text: The horse’s mane flies and its nostrils steam. Then the opening pace returns in a single step. Muted violins and harp restore the sunlight on the water; Thorborg repeats the words “Gold’ne Sonne” — golden sun.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 77, rehearsal 16: Tempo I subito (Andante), muted violins and the return of “Gold’ne Sonne webt um die Gestalten”. Our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A glance that lingers
cues.text: The girl’s proud bearing is a pretence. Her eyes follow the rider, and her heart still trembles after he has gone. Mahler writes “Ganz ruhig” — quite calm — while clarinet phrases and the violins carry on beneath Thorborg’s last words.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 78–80, rehearsal figures 19–22. The final stanza and its quiet clarinet and violin writing; translation of Mahler’s tempo marking.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A conductor who stayed with Mahler
cues.text: Carl Schuricht, born in Danzig in 1880, was Wiesbaden’s music director from 1912. He gave the city the Eighth Symphony in 1913 and Mahler weeks in 1920 and 1921. He conducts this performance in Amsterdam on 5 October 1939, when Mahler’s music has vanished from German concert programmes.
cues.evidence: The Wiesbaden Stadtlexikon entry on Schuricht gives his birth in Danzig on 3 July 1880, his appointment as municipal music director in 1912 and his Mahler programmes (the Symphony of a Thousand in 1913, Gustav Mahler weeks in 1920 and 1921): https://www.wiesbaden.de/en/microsite/stadtlexikon/import/a-z/schuricht-carl . The Internet Archive item gives the Amsterdam concert of 5 October 1939: https://archive.org/details/06-das-lied-von-der-erde-mahler-concertgebouw-amsterdam-carl-schuricht-5.-x.-193 . Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay on the 1938 Ninth notes that Mahler’s music was disappearing from concert programmes after a pattern set in Germany: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

transitions.title: The violins uncover E major
transitions.from: A · Lotus flowers beside the river
transitions.to: B · The breeze lifts silk sleeves
transitions.how: A ritardando ends the image of sunlight reflected in water. The music resumes in E major, a minor third below G, at a tempo (ruhiger). The violins take off their mutes; their high melody and the woodwinds’ little turns prepare the breeze stanza.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 63–64, rehearsal 5: E-major signature, a tempo (ruhiger), Dämpfer ab and solo violin.

transitions.title: The singer leaves the horses approaching
transitions.from: B · The breeze lifts silk sleeves
transitions.to: C · Horsemen approach in the orchestra
transitions.how: After the voice’s final “Luft”, high flute and violin notes hang above the harp. Allmählich belebend sets the orchestra moving: stopped horns, muted trumpet and trombones, with the harp sweeping through D major. The march gathers speed towards its C-major harp glissando.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 65–68, rehearsal figures 7–9: D-major and C-major harp glissandi, brass entries and the march.

transitions.title: Wooden sticks beneath the voice
transitions.from: C · Horsemen approach in the orchestra
transitions.to: D · The singer catches the gallop
transitions.how: The brass-heavy march drops to piano subito. At Noch etwas flotter, Thorborg names the horsemen over oboes, clarinets, bassoons and strings. Timpani played with wooden sticks pick out the rhythm beneath her line.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 70, rehearsal 10: vocal return, p subito, Noch etwas flotter and timpani with Holzschlägel.

transitions.title: Muted violins stop the gallop
transitions.from: D · The singer catches the gallop
transitions.to: A′ · Sunlight returns to the river
transitions.how: The horse’s steaming nostrils end the racing vocal line. Tempo I subito (Andante) brings back muted violins, followed by the harp and a solo violin. The music returns to G major and to the words about golden sunlight on the water.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 77, rehearsal 16. The return begins with two flats before the G-major signature returns in the following system.

transitions.title: The clarinets sustain the last glance
transitions.from: A′ · Sunlight returns to the river
transitions.to: Coda · The girl looks after him
transitions.how: The words about the girl’s pretended pride give way to Ganz ruhig. Quiet violin figures descend while the clarinets exchange short phrases. The final vocal line ends in G major; the winds and strings continue its small gestures into the closing bars.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 79–80, rehearsal figures 19–22: Ganz ruhig, clarinet phrases, violin figures and the orchestral ending.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, IV. Von der Schönheit, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 61–80: the river scene, horsemen’s march and quiet return. The march also includes a mandolin.

timeline.note: Trilling flutes, a horn and muted violins open the song.
The alto enters over soft woodwinds, harp and muted strings.
Ruhiger: piccolo, horn and glockenspiel as the girls gather blossoms.
The violins remove their mutes as E major arrives; harp chords support the woodwinds.
A solo violin rises above the strings at the breeze and the perfumes.
After “Luft”, stopped horns and muted trumpet and trombones enter above a harp glissando.
A C-major harp glissando and brass with open bells open the horsemen’s music.
The march: timpani with wooden sticks, bass drum, tambourine and brass.
Thorborg returns at piano, with woodwinds, strings and timpani played with wooden sticks.
Allegro without voice: flutter-tongued flutes, trombones and tuba, driving strings.
Trumpets raise their bells above the percussion and galloping strings.
The alto returns for the neighing horse, with springing bows in the violins.
Tempo I subito: muted violins, solo violin and harp return with the sun-on-water words.
At Ganz ruhig, quiet violin figures and clarinet phrases accompany Thorborg’s last lines.
The voice has finished; woodwinds and harp carry fragments of the opening theme.
Harp harmonics and low strings leave a final ppp chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Kerstin Thorborg (contralto), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
